front: Can a broker file an entry using a power of attorney from an unlicensed intermediary?
back: A broker may only accept a power of attorney directly from the actual owner, purchaser, or consignee of the merchandise, or from another entity legally authorized to grant it, not from an unlicensed intermediary claiming to represent the importer without proper documentation, under 19 CFR Part 141 Subpart C. The broker must exercise reasonable care in verifying the identity and authority of the party granting the power of attorney. Filing on behalf of a party without a valid power of attorney can expose the broker to liability and disciplinary action.

front: How does the concept of constructive liquidation affect entries under review during litigation?
back: Even while an entry is under protest or litigation at the Court of International Trade, the underlying liquidation, whether original or deemed under 19 USC 1504, generally remains the operative starting point unless and until it is legally overturned or reliquidated pursuant to a final court judgment or granted protest. This means duty liability as originally liquidated stands unless successfully challenged. Importers must still comply with payment obligations pending resolution of a dispute, subject to specific statutory procedures for contesting liability.

front: How does the entry process differ for merchandise arriving by different modes of transportation?
back: While the core entry and entry summary requirements under 19 CFR Parts 141 and 142 apply broadly, certain procedural details differ by mode, such as ISF 10+2 applying only to ocean cargo, and manifest and cargo release procedures for air, truck, and rail having their own specific regulatory provisions. Timeframes for filing entry documentation can also vary depending on mode and whether the shipment arrives via a land border versus a seaport or airport. Brokers must be familiar with mode-specific requirements in addition to the general entry rules.

front: How long can merchandise generally remain in in-bond status?
back: Merchandise transported in-bond must generally be entered or exported within the time limits established for the specific type of in-bond movement, and carriers are responsible for timely delivery. In-bond shipments not properly closed out can trigger liquidated damages against the carrier's bond. CBP tracks in-bond movements electronically through ACE.

front: How long does an importer have to file entry after the merchandise arrives?
back: Entry must generally be filed within 15 calendar days of the date the merchandise arrives within the port limits, under 19 CFR Part 141. Because these are calendar days, weekends and holidays count.

front: How long does an importer have to file the entry summary and deposit estimated duties?
back: The entry summary and the deposit of estimated duties must generally be filed within 10 working days after entry is filed and the merchandise is released, under 19 CFR Part 141. These are working days, meaning business days, which deliberately contrasts with the calendar-day rule for filing entry.

front: How long is a power of attorney generally valid?
back: A power of attorney granted to a customs broker remains valid until revoked, or for corporations, may be limited to two years if signed by a resident partner, officer, or agent under certain circumstances specified in 19 CFR 141.34. Importers can revoke a power of attorney at any time by providing written notice to the broker. Brokers should retain powers of attorney as part of their required recordkeeping.

front: How long may merchandise remain in a bonded warehouse?
back: Merchandise may generally remain in a bonded warehouse for up to five years from the date of importation, under 19 USC 1557. If not withdrawn for consumption, exportation, or transfer within that period, the merchandise is considered unclaimed and may be subject to general order procedures. This five-year period allows importers flexibility in timing duty payment or re-export decisions.

front: How many days does an importer have to file the entry summary after release?
back: The entry summary (CBP Form 7501) and estimated duties must be filed within 10 working days after the merchandise is entered or released, whichever comes first. This deadline is set out in 19 CFR 142.11. Failure to file within this window can result in liquidated damages against the importer's bond.

front: How many one-year extensions of liquidation can CBP take, and up to what total?
back: Under 19 USC 1504, CBP may extend the one-year liquidation period in one-year increments, but the total time before an entry is deemed liquidated by operation of law cannot exceed four years from the date of entry. Extensions are typically granted when CBP needs more information, when antidumping or countervailing duty proceedings are pending, or when the importer requests an extension. CBP must provide notice of each extension to the importer or the importer's broker.

front: Name the 10 importer-side data elements in the ISF.
back: The 10 importer elements include: seller, buyer, importer of record number, consignee number, manufacturer or supplier, ship-to party, country of origin, commodity HTS number, container stuffing location, and consolidator (stuffer). These must be filed with CBP before lading, and the two carrier elements (vessel stow plan and container status messages) are filed separately.

front: What are Partner Government Agencies (PGAs) in the entry process?
back: Partner Government Agencies are federal agencies other than CBP, such as the FDA, USDA, EPA, and Consumer Product Safety Commission, that have jurisdiction over certain imported goods and require additional data or approval before release. PGA data is transmitted electronically through ACE alongside the entry filing. CBP acts as the gatekeeper enforcing PGA admissibility requirements at the border on behalf of these agencies.

front: What deadline applies for filing entry documents after arrival of merchandise?
back: Under 19 CFR 141.68, entry must generally be made within 15 calendar days after the merchandise arrives within the port limits, or general order procedures may apply. This is distinct from the 10-working-day deadline for filing the entry summary after release. Failure to enter goods within this period can result in the merchandise being sent to general order storage.

front: What decisions of CBP are protestable under 19 USC 1514?
back: Protestable decisions include the appraised value of merchandise, the classification and rate of duty, the exclusion of merchandise from entry, the liquidation or reliquidation of an entry, and the refusal to pay a claim for drawback, among others. A protest must identify the specific decision being contested and the grounds for the protest. If a decision is not protestable, or the protest is untimely, CBP will deny the protest without reaching the merits.

front: What happens if estimated duties are not paid within the required time?
back: If estimated duties are not deposited with the entry summary within the required 10 working days, CBP may issue a bill for the amount due and can assess interest on the unpaid balance. Repeated failure to timely deposit duties can result in the importer being placed on a periodic monthly statement removal or other compliance measures, and can trigger liquidated damages against the bond. Timely payment is essential to maintaining good standing with CBP.

front: What happens to general order merchandise if it is not claimed within six months?
back: If general order merchandise is not entered or claimed within six months from the date of importation, CBP is authorized to sell the goods at public auction under 19 USC 1491 and 19 CFR Part 127. Proceeds from the sale are applied first to satisfy duties, taxes, and storage charges, with any remainder held for the importer. Perishable, hazardous, or otherwise unsuitable-for-storage merchandise may be disposed of sooner.

front: What happens to merchandise that is not entered within the 15-calendar-day window?
back: Merchandise not entered within 15 calendar days of arrival, or otherwise unclaimed, becomes general order merchandise. It is taken into CBP custody at a bonded general order warehouse, and merchandise left unclaimed for an extended period can be sold at public auction with the proceeds applied first against unpaid duties, taxes, storage, and other charges.

front: What happens when merchandise is entered but later found to be inadmissible?
back: If merchandise is found inadmissible after entry, due to failure to meet a partner government agency requirement, improper marking, or other legal restriction, CBP may issue a Notice to Redeliver requiring the goods to be returned to CBP custody, or may require exportation or destruction of the merchandise. Failure to comply can lead to liquidated damages against the bond or, in serious cases, seizure. The importer generally bears the cost of any required redelivery, storage, or disposal.

front: What information must appear on CBP Form 3461?
back: CBP Form 3461 requires information such as the entry number, importer of record number, port code, bill of lading or airway bill number, importing carrier, manufacturer identification code, country of origin, and a description sufficient to identify the merchandise for release purposes. It does not require full classification or duty calculation, which is reserved for the entry summary. This form is what CBP reviews to decide whether to release cargo, hold it for examination, or refer it to another government agency.

front: What is 19 USC 1520(c) relief, historically, and how has it changed?
back: Historically, 19 USC 1520(c) allowed CBP to reliquidate an entry to correct a clerical error, mistake of fact, or inadvertence discovered within one year of liquidation, even without a timely protest, though this provision was later repealed by the Miscellaneous Trade and Technical Corrections Act of 2004. Today, correcting most errors after liquidation generally requires a timely protest under 19 USC 1514. Brokers should be aware that the 1520(c) remedy is largely no longer available for entries liquidated after the repeal took effect.

front: What is a bonded warehouse and what are its classes?
back: A bonded warehouse is a secure facility approved by CBP where imported merchandise can be stored, manipulated, or manufactured without payment of duty until the goods are withdrawn. CBP recognizes eleven classes of bonded warehouses under 19 CFR Part 19: Class 1 through Class 11, including storage, manufacturing, smelting and refining, and general order classes. Class 5 covers grain storage, Class 6 covers manufacturing in bond, Class 8 covers cleaning, sorting, repacking, or otherwise changing condition but not manufacturing, Class 10 is reserved and unused, and Class 11 is the general order warehouse class. Operators must obtain a permit and meet the bonding requirements that apply to their operations.

front: What is a CBP Form 28?
back: CBP Form 28 is a Request for Information, issued by CBP to an importer to obtain additional documentation or clarification needed to properly process, classify, or value an entry, often before liquidation. A timely and complete response can help avoid a CBP Form 29 Notice of Action proposing a rate advance or other adverse change. Importers and brokers should respond within the time specified, typically 30 days, to preserve their rights.

front: What is a CBP Form 29?
back: CBP Form 29 is a Notice of Action, used by CBP to inform an importer of a proposed or final change to the entry, such as a rate advance, reclassification, or revaluation, along with the reasons for the change. A proposed notice generally gives the importer an opportunity to respond before the action becomes final. If the importer disagrees with a final Notice of Action after liquidation, the remedy is to file a protest under 19 USC 1514.

front: What is a Certificate of Delivery or Certificate of Manufacture and Delivery used for in relation to entry and drawback?
back: A Certificate of Delivery or Certificate of Manufacture and Delivery is a supporting document used to transfer the right to claim drawback from an importer to a subsequent party who exports or uses the merchandise, when that party was not the original importer of record. These certificates help establish the chain of custody needed to support a drawback claim tied back to the original entry. They are retained as part of the required drawback recordkeeping.

front: What is a certified weigher or gauger's role in the entry process?
back: A certified weigher or gauger is an entity accredited by CBP to perform official weighing or gauging of bulk or other commodities where quantity determination affects duty assessment, such as certain agricultural or petroleum products. These certified measurements are used on the entry summary to establish the dutiable quantity. Accreditation and oversight of weighers and gaugers are covered under 19 CFR Part 151.

front: What is a consumption entry?
back: A consumption entry is the most common entry type, used when merchandise is imported for use, sale, or consumption in the United States commerce. It requires the filer to declare classification, value, and pay applicable duties, taxes, and fees. Entry type code 01 is used for consumption entries under normal duty rates.

front: What is a Continuous Bond?
back: A Continuous Bond covers all of an importer's entries over a one-year period and automatically renews unless terminated by the importer or the surety. Continuous bonds are typically set at a minimum of 50,000 dollars or 10 percent of duties, taxes, and fees paid in the prior year, whichever is greater. Most regular importers use continuous bonds because they are more cost-effective than obtaining a new bond for every shipment.

front: What is a drawback claim in relation to entry?
back: Drawback is a refund of certain duties, taxes, and fees paid on imported merchandise that is subsequently exported or destroyed, or used in the manufacture of an exported article, authorized under 19 USC 1313. Drawback claims are filed electronically in ACE and reference the underlying import entries. TFTEA modernized drawback in 2016, generally allowing claims to be filed up to five years from the date of importation.

front: What is a Duty-Free Entry for personal exemptions distinguished from commercial entries?
back: Personal exemptions, such as those available to returning residents under Chapter 98 and 19 CFR Part 148, allow individuals to bring goods into the United States duty-free up to certain dollar or quantity limits for personal, noncommercial use. Commercial entries, by contrast, are governed by the standard entry and entry summary procedures under 19 CFR Part 141 and 142 regardless of value once a commercial nature is established. The distinction matters because personal exemptions are not generally available to importers acting in a business or trade capacity.

front: What is a Foreign Trade Zone (FTZ) entry?
back: A Foreign Trade Zone is a designated site where merchandise can be stored, manipulated, manufactured, or assembled without being subject to U.S. Customs duty until it enters U.S. commerce. The zone admission itself is requested on CBP Form 214; entry type 06 is the Foreign Trade Zone consumption entry used when merchandise is withdrawn from the zone for consumption in the customs territory. Foreign Trade Zones operate under the Foreign Trade Zones Act of 1934 and are regulated in 19 CFR Part 146. Duty is assessed, and often at a more favorable rate, when goods leave the zone for domestic consumption.

front: What is a formal entry?
back: A formal entry is generally required for commercial shipments valued over 2,500 dollars and requires a CBP bond, detailed classification, valuation, and compliance with applicable partner government agency requirements. Formal entries are subject to the full entry and entry summary process under 19 CFR Part 142. Certain commodities, such as textiles, may require formal entry regardless of value.

front: What is a Line Release or similar expedited cargo processing program used for?
back: Expedited processing programs allow qualifying, low-risk, repetitive shipments to be released more quickly by using pre-established data on file with CBP, reducing the need to resubmit full documentation for every shipment. These programs are often used at land border crossings for high-volume, regular importers. They complement, but do not replace, the underlying entry and entry summary filing requirements.

front: What is a live entry?
back: A live entry requires the importer or broker to file the complete entry summary, including classification, value, and payment of estimated duties, at the same time as the entry documentation, rather than allowing the standard 10 working day period to file the summary afterward. Live entry is required for certain commodities, such as those subject to antidumping or countervailing duty orders, or at the discretion of the port director. This ensures duty liability and admissibility issues are resolved before release.

front: What is a Manufacturer Identification Number (MID)?
back: A Manufacturer Identification Number is a code derived from the name and address of the foreign manufacturer or shipper, constructed according to a formula in 19 CFR 102.0 and CBP guidance, and is required on entry documentation to identify the source of the merchandise. The MID helps CBP with targeting, statistical reporting, and enforcement of trade remedies such as antidumping duties. An incorrect MID can cause entry rejection or delay.

front: What is a Notice to Redeliver, and what does it require?
back: A Notice to Redeliver is issued by CBP demanding the return of merchandise that was conditionally released but later found to violate a legal requirement, such as improper marking, failure to meet PGA requirements, or other admissibility issues. Failure to redeliver the merchandise within the specified time can result in liquidated damages up to the full value of the merchandise under the bond. Redelivery notices are typically issued within 30 days of the CBP determination that redelivery is required, though timeframes can vary.

front: What is a Periodic Monthly Statement (PMS)?
back: A Periodic Monthly Statement allows importers to consolidate payment of estimated duties, taxes, and fees for multiple entry summaries filed during a calendar month into a single payment due on a set statement date, typically the 15th business day of the following month. PMS is processed through ACE and offers importers cash flow benefits compared to paying duties entry by entry. Participation requires enrollment and use of Automated Clearing House payment.

front: What is a Post Summary Correction (PSC)?
back: A Post Summary Correction is an electronic filing in ACE that allows an importer or broker to correct entry summary data, such as classification or value, after the entry summary has been filed but before liquidation. PSCs replace the older Post Entry Amendment process and can be used to request either a refund or to pay additional duties owed. PSCs must generally be filed prior to, or up to 15 days before, the scheduled liquidation date.

front: What is a prior disclosure under 19 USC 1592?
back: A prior disclosure is a voluntary written statement made by an importer to CBP disclosing the circumstances of a violation of the customs laws, such as an undervaluation or misclassification, before CBP has begun a formal investigation of the violation. A valid prior disclosure limits the importer's monetary penalty exposure to the interest on unpaid duties (for negligence or gross negligence) rather than the full penalty otherwise authorized under 19 USC 1592. Prior disclosures must be made before CBP has commenced a formal investigation and before the importer had notice that CBP was aware of the violation.

front: What is a protest under 19 USC 1514?
back: A protest is the formal administrative mechanism by which an importer challenges a CBP decision, such as classification, valuation, rate of duty, or exclusion of merchandise, after liquidation. Protests must generally be filed within 180 days after the date of liquidation under 19 USC 1514(c)(3). Protests are filed on CBP Form 19 and are decided by the port director or another designated CBP official.

front: What is a Single Transaction Bond (STB)?
back: A Single Transaction Bond is a bond that covers only one specific entry or transaction, as opposed to a continuous bond, which covers all entries made by an importer over a one-year period. STBs are often used by importers who make infrequent shipments or by entries requiring additional bond coverage beyond a continuous bond amount. The bond amount for an STB is typically set at three times the entered value, or higher for certain regulated commodities.

front: What is a Special Program Indicator (SPI) on an entry summary?
back: A Special Program Indicator, or SPI, is a code entered on CBP Form 7501 to identify merchandise claimed under a special duty program, such as a free trade agreement or a preference program like the Generalized System of Preferences. The SPI is placed with the HTS number to signal the applicable preferential or reduced rate of duty. A USMCA claim uses an SPI on an ordinary consumption entry, not a separate preference entry type. Using an incorrect or unsupported SPI can lead to penalties for false claims of preference.

front: What is a Temporary Importation under Bond (TIB)?
back: A Temporary Importation under Bond, entry type 23, allows merchandise to enter the United States duty-free for a limited time, generally for repair, exhibition, testing, or similar purposes, provided it is exported or destroyed within one year, extendable up to three years total. It is authorized under 19 USC 1202, Chapter 98, Subchapter XIII. The importer posts a bond for double the estimated duties as security for timely exportation.

front: What is a Transportation and Exportation (T&E) entry?
back: A Transportation and Exportation entry permits merchandise to move in-bond from the port of arrival through the United States to a port of exportation without payment of duty, when the goods are ultimately destined for a foreign country. This entry type is often used for cargo moving through the U.S. to Canada or Mexico. No duties are owed because the merchandise never enters U.S. commerce.

front: What is a Vessel Repair Entry?
back: A Vessel Repair Entry, entry type 23 in some contexts or a specialized declaration under 19 USC 1466, applies to equipment, repairs, or materials purchased or obtained for a U.S.-flag vessel in a foreign port, which may be subject to a 50 percent ad valorem duty on the cost of such repairs. This is a specialized entry category distinct from standard merchandise entries. Vessel owners or their agents must declare qualifying foreign repairs upon the vessel's return to the United States.

front: What is a warehouse entry?
back: A warehouse entry, entry type 21, allows merchandise to be placed into a bonded warehouse without payment of duty at the time of entry. Duty is deferred until the goods are withdrawn for consumption, and goods may generally remain in the warehouse up to five years from the date of importation under 19 USC 1557. This entry type is useful for importers who want to defer duty payment or re-export goods without ever paying duty.

front: What is Accelerated Disposition of a protest?
back: Accelerated Disposition allows an importer to request that CBP decide a protest within 30 days of the request, and if CBP fails to act within that period, the protest is deemed denied by operation of law, allowing the importer to proceed to litigate at the Court of International Trade. This procedure is available under 19 CFR 174.22. It is a tool importers use to avoid indefinite delay in obtaining a decision on a protest.

front: What is ACE?
back: ACE stands for the Automated Commercial Environment, the primary system used by CBP and the trade community to process imports and exports electronically. ACE is the single window through which importers, brokers, and other government agencies transmit and access trade data. Nearly all entry types and entry summaries today are filed electronically through ACE.

front: What is ACE and why does it matter to a broker?
back: ACE is the Automated Commercial Environment, CBP's single window system through which importers, brokers, and other agencies electronically process import and export data. It replaced the older Automated Commercial System and is mandated for entry summary filing across virtually all entry types. Brokers use it both to file and to monitor entry status, liquidation status, and bond sufficiency.

front: What is an Immediate Transportation entry used for?
back: An Immediate Transportation entry moves merchandise under bond from the port of arrival to another port, where formal entry will be filed later. It is one of the transportation entry types used when the importer's business or storage location sits away from the port of first arrival.

front: What is an Immediate Transportation (IT) entry?
back: An Immediate Transportation entry allows merchandise arriving at one port to be transported in-bond to another port of entry where the formal entry will actually be filed. The merchandise is not appraised or classified at the port of arrival. This entry type is commonly used when goods must be delivered to an inland port closer to the importer's facility.

front: What is an in-bond movement?
back: An in-bond movement is the movement of merchandise under bond, with duties not yet paid, from the port where it arrived to another CBP-designated location, such as a bonded warehouse or a foreign trade zone.

front: What is an informal entry and what is its dollar threshold?
back: An informal entry is a simplified entry procedure generally used for shipments valued at 2,500 dollars or less, though certain commodities have different thresholds. Informal entries require less documentation than formal entries and do not require a surety bond in most cases. CBP officers may also elect to process higher-value shipments as informal entries at their discretion under 19 CFR 143.21.

front: What is CBP Form 3461 used for?
back: CBP Form 3461 is the Entry/Immediate Delivery form used to request release of merchandise from CBP custody before the entry summary is filed. It allows the importer or broker to obtain physical release of goods while the full entry summary documentation and duty payment follow later. It is filed under 19 CFR 142.3 and is the standard release document for most consumption entries filed through ACE.

front: What is CBP Form 7501?
back: CBP Form 7501 is the Entry Summary, the document that declares the final classification, value, and duty owed on imported merchandise. It is filed to finalize the entry after release and serves as the basis for duty collection and statistical reporting. Under 19 CFR 142.11, the entry summary must be filed and estimated duties deposited within 10 working days of the entry of merchandise.

front: What is CBP Form 7501 and what does it declare?
back: CBP Form 7501 is the entry summary. It declares the tariff classification under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, the country of origin, the value for duty purposes, the applicable rate of duty, any preferential trade program claimed, and the total estimated duties, taxes, and fees owed. It is also the vehicle through which the importer pays estimated duties.

front: What is deemed liquidation?
back: Deemed liquidation happens when CBP does not liquidate an entry within the statutory period, which is one year from the date of entry under 19 USC 1504(a)(1) and 19 CFR 159.11(a). There is no 314-day rule. If CBP takes no action and no valid extension applies, the entry is deemed liquidated by operation of law at the rate, value, and classification the importer asserted at entry. This rule gives importers certainty that a transaction will not stay open indefinitely.

front: What is Further Review of a protest?
back: Further Review is a request, made at the time of filing a protest using CBP Form 19, asking CBP Headquarters or a higher authority to review a protest decision rather than having it decided solely at the port level, typically because the issue involves a matter of first impression or conflicts with an existing CBP ruling. Further Review is governed by 19 CFR 174.24 and 174.25. It is used when the importer believes the port's initial decision may not adequately consider a legal or policy issue.

front: What is general order (G.O.) merchandise?
back: General order merchandise is cargo that has not been entered within the time allowed by law, typically 15 calendar days after arrival, and is placed into the custody of a bonded general order warehouse. The importer remains responsible for storage, handling, and any applicable duties. If not entered and claimed within six months from the date of importation, the merchandise may be sold at public auction under 19 USC 1491.

front: What is Immediate Exportation (IE)?
back: Immediate Exportation is an entry procedure used when merchandise arrives at a U.S. port and is intended for prompt export without entering U.S. commerce, without first moving in-bond to another domestic port. It differs from T&E in that the exportation occurs from the same port of arrival. It is governed under 19 CFR Part 18 along with the other in-bond entry types.

front: What is in-bond movement?
back: In-bond movement allows merchandise to move under bond from one port to another, or from the port of arrival to a bonded warehouse or foreign trade zone, without formal entry or payment of duty at the port of arrival. Common in-bond entry types include Immediate Transportation (IT), Transportation and Exportation (T&E), and Immediate Exportation (IE). These movements are governed by 19 CFR Part 18 and must be reported in ACE.

front: What is liquidation of an entry?
back: Liquidation is the final computation or ascertainment of duties, taxes, and fees owed on an entry, marking the point at which CBP's assessment becomes final absent a timely protest or other legal challenge. Liquidation is governed by 19 USC 1500 and 19 CFR Part 159. Once an entry liquidates, the importer's ability to change classification or value generally ends except through a protest.

front: What is Merchandise Processing Fee (MPF)?
back: The Merchandise Processing Fee is an ad valorem fee, generally 0.3464 percent of the entered value for formal entries, subject to statutory minimum and maximum amounts, assessed to fund CBP's processing of commercial entries. Informal entries are assessed a flat MPF amount instead of the ad valorem rate. MPF is collected on the entry summary along with duties and other applicable fees.

front: What is Reconciliation in the ACE system?
back: Reconciliation is an electronic program that allows importers to file entry summaries using estimated information for certain elements, such as value, classification, or free trade agreement eligibility, and later file a Reconciliation entry to provide the final, corrected data. It is authorized under 19 USC 1401 and 19 CFR Part 163, and is particularly useful for related-party transactions where final transfer prices are not known at entry. Reconciliation entries must generally be filed within 21 months of the underlying entry summary date.

front: What is responsible supervision and control?
back: Responsible supervision and control is the standard imposed on licensed customs brokers under 19 CFR 111.1 and 111.28, requiring brokers to actively oversee the customs business conducted by their employees and any unlicensed staff to ensure compliance with customs laws and regulations. Factors CBP considers include training, availability of the broker to employees, and review of transactions. Failure to exercise responsible supervision can result in license suspension or revocation.

front: What is the 15-day rule for entry after arrival, and what triggers general order status?
back: Under 19 CFR 141.68 and related provisions, merchandise must generally be entered within 15 calendar days after arrival within the limits of a port; failure to do so causes the goods to be sent to a general order warehouse at the risk and expense of the importer. This rule ensures cargo does not remain indefinitely uncleared at the port and creates an incentive for importers to file timely entries. Certain circumstances, such as perishable or live merchandise, may trigger a shorter timeframe for disposition.

front: What is the (a)(1)(A) list in customs recordkeeping?
back: The (a)(1)(A) list, published by CBP pursuant to 19 USC 1508(c)(1), identifies the specific categories of records that must be maintained by importers, brokers, and other parties engaged in customs business, such as entry documents, invoices, and records of merchandise. Failure to produce records on this list when demanded can result in monetary penalties under 19 USC 1509. The list is periodically updated by CBP through Federal Register notice.

front: What is the deadline for filing a Post Summary Correction?
back: A Post Summary Correction must generally be filed no later than 15 calendar days before the scheduled liquidation date of the entry summary, in accordance with CBP's ACE PSC guidance. Once liquidation occurs, the importer's remedy shifts from PSC to filing a protest under 19 USC 1514, provided the protest is timely. This timing rule is why importers must monitor scheduled liquidation dates closely.

front: What is the deemed liquidation rule for entries?
back: Under 19 USC 1504(a)(1) and 19 CFR 159.11(a), most entries must be liquidated within one year of the date of entry. There is no 314-day rule, and practitioners should not rely on any shortened period. If CBP does not liquidate and no valid extension applies, the entry is deemed liquidated by operation of law at the rate, value, and classification the importer asserted at entry. CBP may extend the one-year period for specified reasons, such as a pending antidumping or countervailing duty proceeding, a protest, or a request for information.

front: What is the difference between an entry filed under a single entry bond and one filed under a continuous bond in terms of importer obligations?
back: Under either bond type, the importer's underlying legal obligations to file a timely and accurate entry summary and pay duties remain the same, but the bond determines the source and amount of financial security backing those obligations for a given entry or set of entries. A continuous bond covers unlimited entries during its term up to the bond's activity limit, while a single transaction bond only secures one shipment. Importers with frequent shipments generally find a continuous bond more practical and cost-effective.

front: What is the difference between arrival and entry?
back: Arrival happens when the vessel, aircraft, truck, or train physically reaches the United States and reports to CBP. Entry is a separate, formal legal act: the filing of documentation that declares what the merchandise is, who owns it, what it is worth, and what duty rate applies. Merchandise is not legally released for use until CBP authorizes release.

front: What is the difference between entry and entry summary?
back: Entry refers to the documentation and process required to obtain release of merchandise from CBP custody, typically accomplished using CBP Form 3461. Entry summary refers to the subsequent filing, on CBP Form 7501, that provides the complete declaration of classification, value, and duty calculation and triggers payment of estimated duties. The two can be filed simultaneously in some cases, but the entry summary is what CBP uses to liquidate the entry.

front: What is the difference between the port of unlading and the port of entry?
back: The port of unlading is the location where merchandise is physically discharged from the importing carrier, while the port of entry is the CBP port where the formal entry documentation is filed and processed, which may be the same location or a different one if the goods move in-bond. Both are reported separately on entry documentation. This distinction is important for tracking cargo movement and applying the correct local CBP procedures.

front: What is the difference between the right to make entry and the right to make immediate delivery?
back: The right to make entry generally belongs to the owner or purchaser of the goods, or a party holding an endorsed bill of lading, or a licensed customs broker acting on their behalf, as defined in 19 CFR 141.11. Immediate delivery, requested via CBP Form 3461, is a privilege to obtain physical release of goods prior to full entry summary filing and is not automatically available for all entry types or importers. Certain importers must qualify for or specifically request immediate delivery privileges.

front: What is the difference between unused merchandise drawback and manufacturing drawback?
back: Unused merchandise drawback applies when imported merchandise is exported or destroyed without being used in the United States, allowing recovery of up to 99 percent of duties paid. Manufacturing drawback applies when imported merchandise is used to manufacture or produce an article that is then exported, also allowing recovery of up to 99 percent of applicable duties. Both are authorized under 19 USC 1313 and were significantly streamlined by the Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2016.

front: What is the effect of filing an incomplete or inaccurate entry summary?
back: Filing an incomplete or inaccurate entry summary can result in CBP rejecting the filing, delaying liquidation, requesting additional information via CBP Form 28, or in cases of material inaccuracy, pursuing a penalty action under 19 USC 1592. Brokers have an obligation to exercise reasonable care in preparing entry summaries based on information reasonably available to them. Correcting errors before CBP identifies them, through a Post Summary Correction or prior disclosure, generally reduces exposure compared to CBP discovering the error independently.

front: What is the effect of reliquidation on an entry?
back: Reliquidation is a correction to an entry's liquidation, which CBP may initiate on its own within 90 days of the original liquidation to correct a clerical error, mistake of fact, or other inadvertence not amounting to an error in the construction of law, under 19 USC 1520, or as a result of a granted protest. Once reliquidated, the new liquidation becomes the operative final determination, subject to its own protest rights if applicable. Reliquidation cannot generally be used to reopen a legal interpretation the importer failed to timely protest.

front: What is the entry filer's responsibility regarding reasonable care?
back: Under 19 USC 1484, the importer of record is responsible for using reasonable care to enter, classify, and value merchandise, and to provide any other information necessary for CBP to properly assess duties, collect accurate statistics, and determine whether other applicable legal requirements are met. Reasonable care is a flexible standard evaluated based on the importer's experience, the complexity of the transaction, and reliance on qualified experts such as licensed customs brokers. Failure to exercise reasonable care can lead to penalties under 19 USC 1592.

front: What is the entry summary's role in Section 232 or Section 301 duty assessments?
back: For merchandise subject to Section 232 (national security) or Section 301 (unfair trade practices) additional duties, the entry summary must include the applicable additional HTS classification numbers, generally found in Chapter 99, along with the standard classification, to ensure the correct additional duty is assessed. Filing without the required Chapter 99 number can result in underpayment of duty and subsequent CBP action. These trade remedy duties are collected in addition to normal ad valorem duty rates.

front: What is the Harbor Maintenance Fee (HMF)?
back: The Harbor Maintenance Fee is an ad valorem fee of 0.125 percent of the value of commercial cargo imported through certain U.S. ports, used to fund harbor maintenance and dredging. It applies to shipments entering by vessel and is collected on the entry summary alongside duties and MPF. HMF does not apply to air or land shipments.

front: What is the Importer Security Filing, and who files its elements?
back: The Importer Security Filing, also called ISF or 10+2, is the advance electronic security information CBP requires for cargo arriving by vessel. The importer or its agent files 10 data elements and the ocean carrier files 2 more, for a combined 12-element advance filing made before the cargo is laden.

front: What is the Importer Security Filing, or ISF?
back: The Importer Security Filing, commonly called 10+2, requires importers to submit 10 data elements and carriers to submit 2 additional data elements before cargo is laden aboard a vessel destined for the United States. It applies to ocean cargo only, not air or land shipments, and is authorized under the SAFE Port Act of 2006. It must generally be filed no later than 24 hours before the cargo is loaded at the foreign port.

front: What is the North American Free Trade Agreement's successor for preferential entry claims?
back: The United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or USMCA, entered into force on July 1, 2020 and replaced NAFTA. It provides preferential duty treatment for qualifying originating goods traded among the United States, Mexico, and Canada, supported by a certification of origin that may be completed by the importer, exporter, or producer. A USMCA preference claim is made on an ordinary consumption entry by reporting the special program claim indicator on the entry summary. It is not made by using a separate free trade agreement or preference entry type.

front: What is the purpose of a bonded cartman or bonded carrier in the movement of entered or in-bond merchandise?
back: A bonded cartman or bonded carrier is a transportation company licensed and bonded by CBP to move merchandise, including in-bond shipments, general order merchandise, or goods under CBP supervision, between ports, warehouses, or other secure locations without loss of CBP custody or control. These carriers must comply with recordkeeping and reporting requirements under 19 CFR Part 112 and related provisions. Using an unbonded or unauthorized carrier for such movements can result in violations and penalties.

front: What is the purpose of an entry number?
back: The entry number is a unique 11-character identifier assigned to each entry filed with CBP, consisting of a filer code, a serial number, and a check digit. It is used to track the entry throughout the entry, entry summary, and liquidation process, and appears on both CBP Form 3461 and CBP Form 7501. The entry number allows CBP, brokers, and importers to reference a specific transaction across all related documentation.

front: What is the purpose of Census Warning messages during ACE filing?
back: Census Warning messages are automated system alerts generated during ACE entry summary transmission when the reported data, such as quantity or value, falls outside expected statistical parameters for the declared classification, prompting the filer to verify the accuracy of the data before or after submission. These warnings are informational and generally do not prevent filing, but they help catch potential data entry errors. Ignoring recurring Census Warnings without investigation could suggest a lack of reasonable care in entry preparation.

front: What is the purpose of the entry filer code?
back: The entry filer code is a three or four character alphanumeric code assigned by CBP to each licensed customs broker or self-filing importer, used as part of the unique entry number to identify who filed a given entry. It allows CBP to track filing volume, performance, and compliance by filer. The filer code is a component embedded in the broader 11-digit entry number structure.

front: What is the role of a licensed customs broker in entry filing?
back: A licensed customs broker is authorized under 19 USC 1641 to transact customs business on behalf of importers, including preparing and filing entries, entry summaries, and other required documentation with CBP. Brokers must exercise responsible supervision and control over their employees and agents who handle customs business. Only a licensed and permitted broker, or the importer itself, may file entries with CBP.

front: What is the role of the entry summary in statistical reporting?
back: The entry summary, filed via CBP Form 7501, provides the detailed classification, quantity, and value data that CBP and the U.S. Census Bureau use to compile official import trade statistics. Accurate reporting of the 10-digit Harmonized Tariff Schedule number and quantity in the correct units of measure is essential for reliable statistics. Errors in statistical reporting can also trigger compliance scrutiny even if duty liability is unaffected.

front: What is the role of the importer of record?
back: The importer of record is the party responsible for the declaration of merchandise entering the United States, including accurate classification, valuation, and payment of duties, taxes, and fees. The importer of record can be the owner, purchaser, or a licensed customs broker designated by the owner or purchaser under 19 CFR 141.11. The importer of record must possess a valid importer number, typically an IRS employer identification number or CBP-assigned number.

front: What is the role of the surety in the entry process?
back: The surety is the company that issues the customs bond guaranteeing performance of the importer's obligations, including payment of duties, taxes, and fees, and compliance with other customs requirements. If the importer fails to meet its obligations, such as timely filing an entry summary or paying duties, CBP can make a claim against the bond, and the surety becomes liable up to the bond amount. Sureties are regulated and must be listed on the Treasury Department's approved list to issue federal bonds.

front: What is the significance of 19 CFR 141.61 regarding entry summary content?
back: 19 CFR 141.61 specifies the required content and completeness standards for entry summary documentation, including the necessity of a complete and accurate description, classification, and valuation of the merchandise. It establishes that the entry summary must be prepared with reasonable care and contain all information necessary for CBP to properly assess duty and collect statistics. This regulation underlies the day-to-day standards brokers must meet when preparing CBP Form 7501.

front: What is the significance of Automated Clearing House (ACH) in duty payment?
back: The Automated Clearing House is an electronic payment method that allows importers and brokers to pay estimated duties, taxes, and fees directly from a bank account through ACE, rather than by check or other manual method. ACH payment is required for participation in Periodic Monthly Statement processing. Electronic payment methods like ACH have become the standard way duties are remitted to CBP in the modern entry process.

front: What is the significance of country of origin marking on entry documentation?
back: Under 19 USC 1304, imported articles must generally be marked with their country of origin in a conspicuous, legible, and permanent manner to inform the ultimate purchaser, and the entry documentation must accurately reflect that origin. If goods reach liquidation improperly marked, 19 USC 1304(i) imposes an additional marking duty of 10 percent ad valorem, separate from any regular duty owed, unless the goods were exported, destroyed, or properly marked under CBP supervision before liquidation. Under 19 CFR 134.35(a), an imported article used in a US manufacturing process that results in a new article of commerce is excepted from marking, but the outermost containers in which the imported article arrived must still be marked with its foreign origin. Country of origin also affects duty rates, eligibility for trade preference programs, and the applicability of trade remedy orders.

front: What is the significance of the 19 CFR Part 141 general provisions on entry?
back: 19 CFR Part 141 sets out the general requirements for entry of merchandise, including who may make entry, the right to make entry, required documentation, and time limits for entry and entry summary filing. It establishes that entry may be made by the owner, purchaser, or a licensed customs broker with proper authorization. This part forms the regulatory backbone underlying most day-to-day entry filing procedures referenced throughout the CBLE.

front: What is the significance of the date of entry for duty rate purposes?
back: The applicable rate of duty and other requirements are generally determined by the law in effect on the date of entry, or the date of withdrawal from warehouse for consumption if the goods were warehoused, under 19 USC 1505 and related provisions. This is important because tariff rates, quotas, and trade remedy orders can change over time. The date of entry therefore fixes which set of rules governs the transaction.

front: What is the significance of the entered value on CBP Form 7501?
back: The entered value is the declared value of the imported merchandise used as the basis for calculating ad valorem duties, and it must be determined according to the valuation methods set out in 19 USC 1401a, generally starting with transaction value. An inaccurate entered value, whether too high or too low, can result in over or underpayment of duty and potential penalties under 19 USC 1592. The entered value appears on the entry summary alongside the applicable HTS classification and rate of duty.

front: What is the significance of the entry type code on CBP Form 7501?
back: The entry type code is a two-digit number on CBP Form 7501 that identifies the specific kind of entry being filed. Code 01 is the ordinary consumption entry, 02 is consumption for quota or visa merchandise, 03 is consumption for antidumping and countervailing duty merchandise, 06 is a Foreign Trade Zone consumption entry, and 07 is consumption for quota plus antidumping and countervailing duty merchandise. There is no tariff-rate-quota entry type, and entry type 08 is not a free trade agreement or preference entry type. A free trade agreement claim, such as USMCA, is made by reporting the special program claim indicator on a consumption entry. Entry type 09 is the Reconciliation entry.

front: What is the significance of the port of entry on the entry documents?
back: The port of entry identifies the specific CBP port where the merchandise is entered and where the entry and entry summary are filed and processed. Each port is assigned a unique port code used throughout ACE and on CBP forms. The port of entry may differ from the port of unlading if goods move in-bond to another location before formal entry.

front: What is the time limit for filing a drawback claim under TFTEA?
back: Under the Trade Facilitation and Trade Enforcement Act of 2016, drawback claims must generally be filed within five years of the date of importation of the merchandise on which drawback is claimed. This replaced the prior, more fragmented set of deadlines that varied by drawback type. Claims are filed electronically through ACE.

front: What is Transportation and Exportation?
back: Transportation and Exportation covers merchandise that is merely passing through the United States on its way to another country. It moves under bond and is never entered for consumption in the United States.

front: What must a valid prior disclosure include?
back: A valid prior disclosure must identify the class or kind of merchandise involved, identify the entries affected, or a period of time if entries cannot be readily identified, disclose the specific facts and circumstances of the violation, and disclose (or offer to disclose) the actual loss of revenue, if any, within 30 days or a specified extension period. It must be made in writing to CBP. Once filed, the discloser typically has time to tender the actual loss of revenue to perfect the disclosure.

front: What penalty applies for a late or inaccurate ISF filing?
back: CBP may assess liquidated damages of up to 5,000 dollars per violation for a late, inaccurate, or missing ISF filing. Each violation is treated separately, so multiple deficiencies on a single shipment can result in multiple penalties. CBP also has authority to withhold release or delivery of cargo for ISF non-compliance.

front: What penalty framework applies under 19 USC 1592 for fraud versus negligence?
back: Under 19 USC 1592, penalties vary by culpability level: fraud can result in a penalty up to the domestic value of the merchandise, gross negligence up to four times the loss of revenue (or 40 percent of dutiable value if no revenue loss), and negligence up to two times the loss of revenue (or 20 percent of dutiable value if no revenue loss). A valid prior disclosure caps exposure at interest on any unpaid duties for negligence and gross negligence violations. Fraud cases are not eligible for the same reduced penalty treatment even with a prior disclosure, though the interest-only benefit for the duty portion may still apply in some circumstances.

front: What recordkeeping period applies to entry-related records under the customs laws?
back: Under 19 USC 1508 and 19 CFR Part 163, importers and brokers must generally retain records related to an entry for five years from the date of entry, or in the case of drawback, five years from the date of payment of the claim. These records must be made available to CBP upon reasonable request for audit or verification purposes. Failure to produce required records can result in penalties under 19 USC 1509.

front: What role does the bill of lading or airway bill play in the entry process?
back: The bill of lading or airway bill serves as evidence of the right to make entry and provides key shipment information, such as carrier, consignee, and cargo description, that is referenced on CBP Form 3461 to match the entry against the inward cargo manifest. CBP uses this document to verify that the party filing the entry has proper legal authority over the merchandise. An entry cannot generally be processed without the shipment being properly manifested and matched to the entry documentation.

front: What triggers liquidated damages against a bond in the entry context?
back: Liquidated damages are a pre-set monetary amount, specified in the bond conditions, that CBP can assess against the principal and surety when a bonded obligation is breached, such as failing to file the entry summary within 10 working days or failing to redeliver merchandise demanded by CBP. Liquidated damages are not a punitive fine like a 19 USC 1592 penalty but a contractual remedy under the bond. CBP issues a formal notice, CBP Form 5955A, when assessing liquidated damages, and the importer can petition for mitigation.

front: Where does an importer appeal after a protest is denied?
back: After a protest is denied, an importer may file a civil action to contest the denial at the U.S. Court of International Trade (CIT), generally within 180 days after the date of denial under 28 USC 2636(a). The importer must have paid all liquidated duties, taxes, and fees before commencing the action, per 28 USC 2637(a). The Court of International Trade has exclusive jurisdiction over most civil actions arising from CBP protest denials.

front: Which CBP form requests release of merchandise before the entry summary is filed?
back: CBP Form 3461, the Entry or Immediate Delivery application, is the document used to request release of merchandise from CBP custody. Filing it, or its ACE equivalent, is what allows the goods to leave the port before the entry summary and duty payment follow.

front: Which regulations cover informal entry, mail entry, and baggage?
back: The general entry regulations live in 19 CFR Part 141. Informal entry procedures are in 19 CFR Part 143, mail importations are in 19 CFR Part 145, and baggage is in 19 CFR Part 148. Part 143 is not the home of mail or baggage.

front: Why might CBP require a live entry for antidumping or countervailing duty merchandise?
back: CBP often requires live entry for merchandise subject to antidumping or countervailing duty orders because the applicable cash deposit rate must be verified and collected at the time of entry to ensure adequate security against potential duty liability, which can be substantial and case-specific. Waiting the standard 10 days to file the entry summary could allow underpayment or evasion risk on high-duty merchandise. Filing live also allows CBP to catch scope or case number errors before the goods are released into commerce.

front: Are the Explanatory Notes legally binding in the United States?
back: The Explanatory Notes are not legally binding in the United States, but they are generally indicative of the proper interpretation of the Harmonized System and are given considerable weight by CBP and the courts. They are consulted after GRI 1 and the section and chapter notes fail to fully resolve a classification question.

front: At what digit level is the applicable duty rate determined?
back: The applicable duty rate is determined at the eight-digit level of the HTSUS, known as the tariff rate line. The ninth and tenth digits, the statistical suffix, are used solely for statistical reporting purposes and have no effect on the rate of duty owed.

front: Can a binding ruling be relied upon by someone other than the requester?
back: A binding ruling is legally binding only as to the transaction and party for which it was issued, but any importer may use a published ruling covering substantially identical merchandise as persuasive guidance for classifying their own goods. Relying on someone else's ruling does not provide the same legal protection as obtaining one's own ruling for the specific transaction.

front: Can a classifier rely on a competitor's or third party's binding ruling for their own identical merchandise?
back: A published ruling for substantially identical merchandise can be persuasive guidance and is a strong indicator of how CBP would likely classify similar goods, but it does not bind CBP with respect to a different importer's entries. For legal certainty on a specific transaction, the importer should request its own binding ruling.

front: Can an eo nomine provision be limited by a use limitation elsewhere in the tariff?
back: Yes, even though an eo nomine provision names an article specifically, a section or chapter note or the heading language itself can impose a use limitation, meaning the article must actually be used for a stated purpose to qualify, effectively converting or limiting an otherwise name-based provision.

front: Can classification skip GRI 1 and go directly to GRI 3?
back: No, the General Rules of Interpretation must be applied in sequential order, and GRI 1 must be exhausted, including all relevant section and chapter notes, before moving to GRI 2 or GRI 3. Only when GRI 1 fails to resolve the classification, or creates a conflict between two or more headings, does the classifier proceed to the subsequent rules.

front: Define a use provision in tariff classification.
back: A use provision classifies merchandise according to the use to which it is put rather than by its specific name. Use provisions are further divided into principal use provisions, which look at the use of the class or kind of goods as a whole, and actual use provisions, which require proof of the individual item's actual use after importation.

front: Define an eo nomine tariff provision.
back: An eo nomine provision describes an article by its specific name, such as bicycles or hammers, rather than by use or function. Absent contrary legislative intent, an eo nomine provision generally includes all forms of the named article, including improved forms, unless the improved form has a distinct name and use of its own.

front: Does GRI 2(a) apply if the components require further manufacturing rather than mere assembly?
back: No, GRI 2(a) only applies to components that require simple assembly operations, such as fastening with screws or bolts. If the components require additional working or finishing operations, such as cutting, drilling, or machining, before the finished article results, GRI 2(a) does not apply to treat the unfinished parts as the complete article.

front: Explain GRI 3(a), the rule of most specific description.
back: GRI 3(a) provides that the heading which provides the most specific description is preferred over headings providing a more general description. However, when two or more headings each refer to only part of the materials in a mixed or composite good, or to only part of the items in a set, those headings are regarded as equally specific. In that case, classification moves to GRI 3(b).

front: Give an example of how GRI 3(b) is applied to a gift basket.
back: A gift basket containing wine, cheese, and crackers packaged together for a particular occasion would be examined under the three-part set test. If it qualifies as a set, the components are compared to determine which imparts the essential character, often based on which item drives the value, bulk, or the reason a consumer would buy the basket, and the whole set is classified under that heading.

front: How are parts classified when a specific parts provision exists in a chapter?
back: When a section or chapter note or a heading specifically provides for parts of an article, that specific parts provision generally controls classification of the part over a more general residual parts heading. Chapter and section notes frequently address whether parts are classified with the parent article or under their own separate provision.

front: How can CBP modify or revoke a binding ruling?
back: CBP may modify or revoke a binding ruling if it determines the ruling was in error or if circumstances have changed, but it must generally publish notice of the proposed action in the Customs Bulletin and allow a period for public comment before the modification or revocation takes effect. This process is required under 19 USC 1625(c) when the change would have a broad effect on the trade.

front: How do CBP rulings treat kits containing components for multiple different finished articles?
back: CBP examines whether such kits meet the GRI 3(b) set criteria, namely different articles from different headings, put up together to meet a particular need or activity, and packaged for retail sale without repacking. If the kit fails any prong, for example if the components do not work together toward one activity, the kit is not treated as a set and each item may be classified separately.

front: How do chapter notes interact with heading language under GRI 1?
back: GRI 1 requires that classification be determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes, meaning the notes are consulted together with heading language as a single legal inquiry. A chapter note can expand, restrict, or entirely exclude goods from a heading even if the heading's plain language would otherwise seem to cover them.

front: How does a chapter note defining 'parts' as excluding certain machines affect classification analysis order?
back: Such a note must be consulted at the GRI 1 stage, before any parts heading is applied, because it operates as a binding legal exclusion that redirects certain items to a different heading entirely, regardless of how naturally they might otherwise fit the description of a part within that chapter.

front: How does a customs broker's classification duty relate to the reasonable care standard?
back: A licensed customs broker preparing entries must exercise the same reasonable care standard as the importer, using accepted classification methodology, consulting the section and chapter notes and GRIs properly, and seeking a binding ruling or expert guidance when classification is uncertain. Failure to do so can expose both the importer and the broker to penalties.

front: How does GRI 3(a) treat two headings that each cover only part of a composite good?
back: GRI 3(a) provides that when two or more headings each refer only to part of the materials contained in mixed or composite goods, or to only part of the items in a set put up for retail sale, those headings are to be regarded as equally specific with respect to those goods, even if one of them gives a more complete or precise description. In that situation, classification moves on to GRI 3(b).

front: How does 'principal function' differ conceptually from 'essential character'?
back: Principal function is a specific classification concept found in certain section and chapter notes, particularly Section XVI, used to classify composite or combination machines according to which machine performs the primary operational role. Essential character is the broader GRI 3(b) concept applied to mixtures, composite goods generally, and retail sets when no more specific note governs.

front: How does the last rule of GRI 3(c) work in practice?
back: When goods are equally described under two competing headings and neither GRI 3(a) essential specificity nor GRI 3(b) essential character resolves the classification, GRI 3(c) directs classification under whichever competing heading appears numerically last in the tariff schedule. This is a mechanical tiebreaker used only as a last resort.

front: How is the HTSUS organized structurally?
back: The HTSUS is organized into 22 sections, which are divided into 99 chapters. Each chapter is divided into headings, and headings are further divided into subheadings. This hierarchical structure moves from general categories at the section level to increasingly specific product descriptions at the subheading level.

front: How many digits make up an HTSUS classification number?
back: A full HTSUS classification number has 10 digits. The first six digits are the international Harmonized System number, common to all countries that use the HS. The final four digits are US-specific, with digits seven and eight being the tariff rate line and digits nine and ten being the statistical suffix.

front: How should a broker approach classifying a novel or new-to-market product?
back: A broker should research analogous rulings in CROSS, review the relevant section and chapter notes and Explanatory Notes, apply the GRIs sequentially, and if uncertainty remains, recommend the importer request a binding ruling from CBP's National Commodity Specialist Division before finalizing entries, to obtain legal certainty and avoid penalty exposure.

front: Is value always the controlling factor in an essential character determination?
back: No, value is only one of several factors considered in an essential character analysis and is not automatically controlling. CBP and the courts weigh value alongside bulk, quantity, weight, and the functional role of each component, and in some cases a less valuable component that performs the primary function may be found to impart essential character.

front: State General Rule of Interpretation 1 (GRI 1).
back: GRI 1 provides that classification is determined according to the terms of the headings and any relative section or chapter notes. Section and chapter titles are provided for ease of reference only and have no legal weight. GRI 1 is applied first, and if the heading terms and notes resolve classification, no further GRI need be consulted.

front: What are 'goods put up in sets for retail sale' distinguished from mixtures?
back: A mixture involves combining substances or materials, such as a blend of two chemicals, addressed initially through GRI 2(b). A set for retail sale involves multiple distinct articles from different headings packaged together to meet a specific need, addressed under GRI 3(b) once the three set criteria are satisfied. Both are ultimately resolved through the essential character test if GRI 3(a) does not apply.

front: What are the three duty rate columns shown in the HTSUS?
back: The HTSUS displays a General column, a Special column, and Column 2. The General rate applies to countries receiving normal trade relations status. The Special column shows preferential rates available under free trade agreements or preference programs, with program symbols indicating eligibility. Column 2 applies to countries such as Cuba and North Korea that do not receive normal trade relations status.

front: What common law doctrine addresses whether an improved article stays within its original eo nomine provision?
back: Courts generally hold that an eo nomine designation, absent limiting language or contrary legislative intent, includes all forms of the named article, including subsequently developed or improved forms, unless the new form has become so different that it has acquired a distinct name, character, or use of its own.

front: What database allows the public to search published CBP rulings?
back: The Customs Rulings Online Search System, known as CROSS, is CBP's public database that allows anyone to search for published binding rulings by keyword, HTS number, ruling number, or date. It is a key research tool for brokers and importers seeking guidance on how similar merchandise has previously been classified.

front: What does 'akin' mean under GRI 4?
back: Under GRI 4, goods that cannot be classified by application of GRI 1 through 3 are classified under the heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin, meaning most similar in terms of description, purpose, character, and use. This rule is invoked only very rarely because GRI 1 through 3 resolve nearly every classification.

front: What does GRI 2(b) address?
back: GRI 2(b) provides that any reference to a material or substance includes mixtures or combinations of that material with other materials. It also states that any reference to goods of a given material includes goods consisting wholly or partly of that material. When goods consist of more than one material, classification is determined according to GRI 3.

front: What does GRI 4 provide?
back: GRI 4 states that goods which cannot be classified under GRI 1 through 3 are classified under the heading appropriate to the goods to which they are most akin. This is sometimes called the akin goods rule. It is rarely used in practice because GRI 1 through 3 resolve nearly all classification questions.

front: What does GRI 5(a) provide about cases and containers?
back: GRI 5(a) provides that cases and containers specially shaped or fitted to contain a specific article or set of articles, suitable for long-term use, and presented with the articles they are intended to hold, are classified with those articles. This applies to items such as camera cases, musical instrument cases, and gun cases. It does not apply if the container gives the whole its essential character.

front: What does GRI 5(b) provide about packing materials?
back: GRI 5(b) provides that packing materials and packing containers presented with the goods therein are classified with the goods if they are of a kind normally used for packing such goods. This rule does not apply when the packing materials or containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use, such as certain metal drums or reusable containers.

front: What does HTSUS stand for?
back: HTSUS stands for the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States. It is the primary source for determining tariff classifications for goods imported into the United States. It is based on the international Harmonized System maintained by the World Customs Organization, with US-specific statistical suffixes added.

front: What does 'n.e.s.o.i.' mean in the HTSUS?
back: N.e.s.o.i. stands for 'not elsewhere specified or included' and is used to mark residual or basket tariff provisions that capture merchandise not more specifically described by another heading or subheading. It signals that this provision should only apply after all more specific classification options have been ruled out.

front: What does the term 'prima facie classifiable' mean in the context of GRI 3?
back: Prima facie classifiable means that, on its face, a good appears to be properly described by two or more different headings under GRI 1 or GRI 2, creating a genuine conflict that must be resolved. GRI 3 only comes into play once this threshold condition of apparent dual or multiple classifiability has been established.

front: What factors are considered in determining principal use under the Carborundum factors?
back: Courts commonly apply the Carborundum factors to determine principal use, which include the general physical characteristics of the merchandise, the expectation of the ultimate purchaser, the channels of trade in which the merchandise moves, the environment of sale, usage in the same manner as merchandise which defines the class, economic practicality of so using the import, and recognition in the trade of this use.

front: What happens if CBP disagrees with the classification proposed in a binding ruling request?
back: CBP independently analyzes the merchandise and issues its own determination of the correct classification in the ruling letter, which may differ from the classification proposed by the requester. The ruling, once issued, is binding on CBP for future transactions matching the facts described, regardless of which classification the requester originally suggested.

front: What happens when GRI 3(a) and 3(b) both fail to resolve classification?
back: GRI 3(c) then applies as the tiebreaker of last resort. It provides that the good is classified under the heading which occurs last in numerical order among those headings that equally merit consideration. This is a purely mechanical rule applied only after the more substantive tests have failed.

front: What is 9801.00.10, US goods returned?
back: Subheading 9801.00.10 provides duty-free treatment for products of the United States that were exported and are being returned without having been advanced in value or improved in condition while abroad. This provision commonly applies to US-origin goods that were sent abroad and did not sell or were returned unaltered.

front: What is a 'basket' or residual provision in the HTSUS?
back: A basket or residual provision is a tariff line, often containing language such as 'other' or 'not elsewhere specified or included,' that captures goods not more specifically described elsewhere within a heading or chapter. Classifiers should only use a basket provision after confirming that no more specific provision applies.

front: What is a binding ruling under 19 CFR Part 177?
back: A binding ruling is a written decision issued by US Customs and Border Protection in response to a prospective importer's request, addressing questions such as tariff classification, country of origin, or marking requirements for a specific transaction. It is legally binding on CBP for the transaction described and provides the importer with certainty prior to importation.

front: What is a composite good for classification purposes?
back: A composite good consists of two or more different components that are attached to each other to form a practically inseparable whole, or that are separable but adapted to each other and mutually complementary, and which together form a whole that would not normally be offered for sale in separate parts. Composite goods are classified under GRI 3(b) according to their essential character.

front: What is a definitional chapter or section note?
back: A definitional note establishes the legal meaning of a term as it is used throughout a section or chapter, which may differ from the term's common commercial or dictionary meaning. These notes are binding for classification purposes and must be applied whenever the defined term appears within that section or chapter.

front: What is a 'like article produced in the United States' test used for?
back: This phrase and similar language appears in certain use provisions and duty preference programs to compare an imported article to domestically produced goods of the same class or kind, helping determine tariff treatment, quota eligibility, or preference program qualification based on comparability to US production.

front: What is a protest under 19 USC 1514 in relation to classification?
back: A protest is the formal administrative mechanism by which an importer challenges a CBP decision, including a classification decision made at liquidation, within 180 days of liquidation. It must be filed with the port that liquidated the entry and must set out the grounds for the importer's disagreement with CBP's determination.

front: What is a set put up for retail sale under the GRIs?
back: For GRI 3(b) purposes, a set put up for retail sale must consist of at least two different articles classifiable in different headings, must consist of articles put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity, and must be put up in a manner suitable for sale directly to users without repacking. All three conditions must be met for the set rule to apply.

front: What is a 'specially shaped or fitted' container under GRI 5(a)?
back: A specially shaped or fitted container is one manufactured or designed specifically to hold a particular article, such as a violin case molded to the shape of the instrument or a camera case fitted for a specific camera model, rather than a generic container that could hold many different items. Such containers, when imported with the article, are classified together with it.

front: What is a statistical suffix in an HTSUS number?
back: The statistical suffix comprises the ninth and tenth digits of the ten-digit HTSUS classification number and is used by the US Census Bureau and other agencies to collect detailed import statistics. It does not affect the applicable duty rate, which is determined at the eight-digit tariff rate line level.

front: What is Additional US Rule of Interpretation 1(a)?
back: Additional US Rule of Interpretation 1(a) addresses tariff classification controlled by use, providing that a principal use provision covers goods of a class or kind to which the imported good belongs, based on the use of that class or kind in the United States at or immediately prior to the date of importation. The controlling use is that of the class or kind as a whole, not the actual use of the particular imported item.

front: What is Additional US Rule of Interpretation 1(b)?
back: Additional US Rule of Interpretation 1(b) addresses actual use provisions, providing that goods classifiable under an actual use provision must actually be used for the specified purpose, that such use must be intended at the time of importation, and that proof of the use must be furnished within three years after the date the goods are entered.

front: What is an unassembled article under GRI 2(a)?
back: An unassembled article is one whose components are presented together but not yet joined, requiring only assembly operations such as bolting, riveting, or gluing rather than further working or finishing to become a complete article.
